titleText.es: Se puede mejorar mucho ese 1% si empiezas a registrar los patrones que sigue la gente al escoger números.
titleText.en: You can do a lot better than 1% if you start keeping track of the patterns in what numbers people pick.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive credits Gabriel Rodríguez Alberich and closely translates the official title text. Its raster preserves the official four-panel exchange and the final probability caption. Vision found all lexical units but used overlapping full-row rectangles and absorbed commas, periods, question marks, exclamation marks, and ellipses; the checked direct geometry separates those marks.

applications.explanationEn: No negates existe, and tal before cosa identifies the kind of thing whose existence is denied.

regions.labelEs: VALE, PIENSA EN UN NÚMERO DEL UNO AL CIEN.

applications.explanationEn: Piensa supplies the requested mental action, en introduces what should come to mind, and un número fills that thought slot.
Piensa is the positive command used to tell one familiar person to think.
Del combines de with el before the starting endpoint uno, while al combines a with el before the ending endpoint cien.

excludedUnits.rationale: 43 is the guessed numeral, not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: INTENTO QUE NO AFECTE MUCHO A MI VIDA.

applications.explanationEn: Intento names the attempt, que opens its desired result, no negates that result, and ordinary afecta changes to afecte because the effect is a goal rather than an asserted fact.

regions.labelEs: ESPERA, NO ME LO PUEDO CREER.

applications.explanationEn: Espera is the positive command used to tell one familiar person to wait.
No negates puedo, me identifies the reacting speaker, lo stands for the surprising fact, and creer stays unchanged after puedo.
Puedo changes for the speaker, while creer stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the possible action.

regions.labelEs: NO LE PRESTES ATENCIÓN. OLVIDA LO QUE HE DICHO.

applications.explanationEn: No begins the negative instruction, le appears before the verb as its object marker, and ordinary prestas changes to the familiar negative-command form prestes.
Prestes is the changed form of prestar required by the negative instruction, while atención completes the conventional expression.
Olvida is the positive command used to tell one familiar person to forget something.
Lo que points neutrally to an unnamed thing or idea; the following words identify it as previously said content.
He is the helper form for the speaker, and dicho is decir's irregular completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: PUEDE QUE ESTE TRUCO SÓLO FUNCIONE UN 1% DE LAS VECES, PERO CUANDO LO HACE, MERECE COMPLETAMENTE LA PENA.

excludedUnits.rationale: 1% is a numerical probability measurement, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.exampleEs: PUEDE QUE ESTE TRUCO SÓLO FUNCIONE
applications.explanationEn: Puede que opens a possibility, este truco names its subject, sólo limits the claim, and ordinary funciona changes to the possibility form funcione.
Lo stands for the already mentioned action, and hace is the matching present form that avoids repeating that action.
Completa takes its feminine singular form and adds -mente to make completamente, which strengthens the degree here.
Merece and la pena form the conventional value expression, while completamente intensifies how strongly that value is claimed.

cards.answerEn: psychic; a person claimed to perceive thoughts or future events
cards.noteEn: Psíquico can describe supposed powers beyond ordinary senses or name a person who claims to have them. The -o form is masculine singular.

example.es: El supuesto psíquico predijo el resultado.
example.en: The supposed psychic predicted the result.

cards.promptEs: psíquico · número del uno al cien · 1% · patrones al escoger
cards.answerEn: a fixed guess among one hundred numbers has a 1% chance if choices are uniform, while tracking people's non-random choices can improve the odds
cards.noteEn: The man asks for a number from one to one hundred and guesses 43. A uniformly random choice would match that fixed guess one time in a hundred. The title text points out that people favor some numbers over others, so recording their choices could make the trick work more often; the rare success is convincing enough to sustain the false psychic claim.
A speaker can use ¿sabes? to introduce a thought or draw the listener's attention, without literally testing what the listener knows.

example.en: You know? I think you're right.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that no such thing exists?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a matching form of existir, and tal before the kind of thing being denied.
cards.noteEn: Existir changes to match one or more things: no existe tal problema but no existen tales problemas. Tal means “such” before a singular naming word and becomes tales before a plural one.
Before a singular naming word, tal points to something of the kind just mentioned. It becomes tales before a plural naming word.

example.en: I know of no such rule.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: pensar en + persona, cosa o idea
cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone is thinking about?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of pensar followed by en, then name the person, thing, or idea.
cards.noteEn: Pensar changes for the person and time, while en stays in place before what comes to mind. Depending on context, English uses either “think about” or “think of.”

example.en: I am thinking about my friends.

cards.noteEn: Pensar en means to think of or think about someone or something.

cards.answerEn: from the; de + el marking the start of a range
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. In a range, it introduces the starting endpoint when that endpoint uses the masculine article el.

example.es: La oficina abre del lunes al viernes.
example.en: The office opens from Monday to Friday.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a range from one endpoint to another?
cards.answerEn: Put de before the starting point and a before the endpoint.
cards.noteEn: Articles and other determiners stay with each endpoint: de la mejor a la peor; del lunes al viernes. The same frame works for rankings, places, and times.

example.en: She works from Monday to Friday.

cards.answerEn: to the; a + el marking the end of a range
cards.noteEn: Al combines a and el. In a range, it introduces the ending endpoint when that endpoint uses the masculine article el.

example.es: La oficina abre del lunes al viernes.
example.en: The office opens from Monday to Friday.

cards.answerEn: holy shit!; damn! (vulgar exclamation, especially in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Cojones literally names testicles, but by itself it can be a strong vulgar reaction to shock or surprise. It is much stronger than a neutral exclamation.

cards.promptEs: intentar que + otra persona + acción en subjuntivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to get another person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar, then que, name the other person when needed, and put that person's action in its special non-factual form.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It presents the later action as the goal of the attempt rather than an established fact: ordinary abre changes to abra, and ordinary viene changes to venga. If the same person both tries and acts, use intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form instead.

example.en: We try to get Pablo to arrive early.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: affect (special form for an intended or uncertain result)
cards.noteEn: Afecte is a form of afectar used when the effect is presented as a goal, possibility, wish, or other non-established result. The ordinary one-thing form afecta changes its final -a to -e.

example.es: Espero que el ruido no afecte al bebé.
example.en: I hope the noise does not affect the baby.

cards.noteEn: Mucho can stand by itself when the kind of amount is already clear. It then means ‘much’ or ‘a lot’ without a following noun.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces what is affected
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses afectar a before the person, thing, or area receiving an effect. Natural English normally puts that target directly after “affect.”

example.es: El retraso afecta a todo el proyecto.
example.en: The delay affects the whole project.

cards.questionEn: How do you express that someone cannot believe something?
cards.answerEn: Use no, then the matching person marker and lo before a form of poder, followed by creer: no se lo puede creer.
cards.noteEn: Me, te, se, nos, or os identifies the person reacting, while lo stands for the surprising fact. Only poder changes for the person and time; creer stays in its unchanged dictionary form. The two markers may instead attach to creer: no puede creérselo.

example.es: Ana no se lo puede creer.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.
Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.promptEs: orden negativa de tú: no + verbo
cards.questionEn: How do you tell one friend or familiar person not to do something?
cards.answerEn: Put no before the verb's special negative-command form. If the verb uses te, put te between no and the verb.
cards.noteEn: For a regular -ar verb, the negative form usually ends in -es: hablar becomes no hables. Regular -er and -ir verbs usually end in -as: comer becomes no comas. A short word such as te goes before this negative form, as in no te levantes.
Here le points back to a thing and functions as an indirect-object pronoun with prestar atención. A fuller a + noun phrase can state what le refers to.

example.es: A esta cuestión le presto mucha atención.
example.en: I pay close attention to this issue.

cards.answerEn: pay (attention; special form in a negative informal command)
cards.noteEn: Prestes comes from prestar. When telling one familiar person not to do something, ordinary prestas changes to no prestes. In prestar atención, prestar means “to pay” attention rather than “to lend.”

example.en: Do not pay attention to the rumor.

cards.noteEn: English uses “pay,” but Spanish uses prestar, a verb that by itself often means “to lend.” Add a before the person or thing receiving the attention: prestar atención a algo.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “to pay attention” in Spanish?

cards.noteEn: Olvida tells one friend, relative, or other familiar person to forget something. It comes from olvidar.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Dicho is the irregular completed-action form of decir, “to say.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “said.”
Vamos is the “we” form of ir, “to go.” Speakers also use it to propose that the group go somewhere or begin moving.
Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.
Eh can fill a pause while a speaker thinks or reacts. Its tone and punctuation determine whether it sounds hesitant, surprised, or attention-getting.

example.en: Um... I need to think about it.

cards.noteEn: Standing alone after a suggestion, venga can show that the speaker accepts or goes along with it. In other contexts it can urge someone on or come from venir, so those senses use separate cards.

cards.answerEn: may; might (as part of puede que)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something may or might be true or happen?
cards.answerEn: Use puede que, then put the following verb in a special possibility form.
cards.noteEn: The special form is called the subjunctive: it presents the following idea as possible rather than as a plain fact. Puede que stays fixed, while the next verb changes to match its own subject; for example, llega becomes llegue and es becomes sea.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes puede que (“may; might”)

cards.noteEn: The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.
Funcione comes from funcionar. After an expression of possibility such as puede que, ordinary funciona changes its final -a to -e because the result is not stated as certain.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish commonly uses un before a percentage
cards.noteEn: A percentage can behave like a masculine quantity in Spanish, so it often follows un: un 20%. Natural English normally says only “20%,” without “a” or “one.”

example.es: Un 20% de los asientos está libre.
example.en: Twenty percent of the seats are free.

cards.noteEn: In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

cards.promptEs: lo + hacer para sustituir una acción anterior
cards.questionEn: How do you avoid repeating an action that was just mentioned?
cards.answerEn: Put lo before a matching form of hacer to mean “do it” or “do so.”
cards.noteEn: Lo stands for the whole earlier action, not for a masculine object, and hacer changes for the person and time: lo hago, lo hace, lo hicieron. The earlier action supplies the meaning that hacer replaces.

example.es: Marta prometió llamar y luego lo hizo.
example.en: Marta promised to call and then did so.

cards.answerEn: does; does so (replacing an earlier action)
cards.noteEn: Hacer normally means “to do” or “to make.” With lo, a form of hacer can stand in for a whole action already mentioned so that the speaker does not repeat that action.

example.es: A veces falla, pero cuando lo hace, avisa.
example.en: Sometimes it fails, but when it does, it gives a warning.

cards.answerEn: is worth (as part of merece la pena)
cards.noteEn: Merece is a form of merecer for one person or thing. The verb can mean “deserves” elsewhere; in merecer la pena, it says that something is worth the time or effort.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is worth the time or effort?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of merecer followed by la pena.
cards.noteEn: Merecer changes for the person, thing, or time, while la pena stays fixed. An action worth doing can follow in its unchanged dictionary form: merece la pena esperar.

example.es: Merece la pena visitar el museo.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.answerEn: effort; completes merecer la pena, “to be worth it”
cards.noteEn: Pena can mean sorrow, pity, or a penalty elsewhere. In the fixed expression merecer la pena, the whole expression means that something is worth the time or effort.
